Research project · SRH Berlin · 2026

A heatsink with no fins.

A 3D-printed copper-alloy lattice for server processors that run fully submerged in coolant, taken from socket drawing to build plate entirely in software.

Design load
2 kW

Design heat load, set well above today's server processors to leave headroom for future chips.

Peak temperature
68.1 °C

Peak temperature in simulation at that load, under the 80 °C design limit.

Compared
4 lattices

Gyroid, diamond, Kelvin cell and honeycomb compared in the same envelope.

Per print job
14 parts

Fit on one EOS M 300-4 build plate per print job.

Why not fins?

Finned heatsinks are shaped for fast-moving air. In an immersion tank the coolant moves slowly and tends to slide past a fin in smooth layers, leaving a warm blanket of fluid on the metal.

A triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) such as the gyroid has no straight channels at all. Every path through it bends, so the coolant keeps mixing. It can only be made by additive manufacturing.

01

Start from the socket

The AMD SP5 socket fixes the 75 × 72 mm contact area and the mounting points. The 2 kW target leaves headroom for future processors and multi-chip modules.

02

Choose the material

CuCrZr conducts heat almost as well as pure copper, is about six times stronger, and prints far more reliably by laser powder bed fusion.

03

Prove it digitally

Lattices modelled in nTopology, flow and temperature simulated, then the build prepared in Netfabb and EOSPRINT. No physical prototype.

Four lattices, one envelope

The honeycomb offers 57% more surface than the gyroid. The gyroid still cools better, because its curved walls reach the highest flow speed and keep stirring the coolant.

Flow decides it

Coolant enters from below and has to find its way through. In the gyroid it is forced around every wall. In the honeycomb it runs straight up the channels and leaves slow zones along the walls.

Temperature at 2 kW

With the full load applied to the baseplate, the CuCrZr gyroid peaks at 68.1 °C. The honeycomb in the same material runs 1.3 °C hotter despite its larger surface.

Pure copper would be about 5 °C cooler but is hard to print. Aluminium runs 15 °C hotter and breaks the 80 °C limit.

Gyroid, Cu 1010062.7 °C
Gyroid, CuCrZr68.1 °C
Honeycomb, CuCrZr69.4 °C
Gyroid, Al 6061-T683.1 °C
0 °CDesign limit 80 °C90

Prepared for printing

The gyroid is largely self-supporting, so supports are only needed near the base. Orientation, supports and nesting were set up in Netfabb, then sliced with process parameters in EOSPRINT.

The planned post-processing covers powder removal from the internal channels, stress relief, solution annealing and ageing to recover conductivity, machining of the mounting faces, and a CT scan.

What is still open

Everything here is simulation. Nothing has been printed or measured yet.

  • Print and test oneMeasure temperature and pressure drop in a real immersion tank.
  • Model the printed surfaceAdd roughness, porosity and direction-dependent conductivity from CT data.
  • Include the chip interfaceThermal paste and contact resistance are left out of the current model.
  • Scale up to a rackSeveral heatsinks sharing one tank, pump and coolant loop.

University project · SRH Berlin · 2025

From a picture to a robot program.

A Python pipeline that turns an image of a shape into a ready-to-run drawing program for an igus ReBeL 6-axis arm, with no points taught by hand.

Pipeline
6 stages

From image file to robot program, all in one script.

Tested
4 shapes

Triangle, square, circle and star, each run in simulation.

Joint limit
140°

Joint 3 stays below this angle. Where it would not, the pen height is raised.

Taught by hand
0 points

Every position in the program comes from the script.

Image in, program out

Teaching a robot a drawing point by point is slow, and every new shape starts from zero. The goal was an arm that draws any outline straight from an image.

01

Load and threshold

Read the image in greyscale and convert it to black and white to isolate the shape.

02

Extract the contour

OpenCV finds the full outer contour, keeping every point so complex outlines stay faithful.

03

Smooth the path

A SciPy spline turns the raw contour into a continuous path the arm can follow without jerks at sharp corners.

04

Scale and centre

Fit the shape's bounding box into the reachable X and Y range and centre it relative to the robot base.

05

Check the joints

Estimate the joint 3 angle from each point's distance to the base. Where it would pass 140°, raise Z to ease the elbow.

06

Write the program

Store every point as a named position, then chain linear moves: approach, pen down, trace, close the shape, lift.

Four programs, plotted

These are the tool paths read back out of the generated XML files, drawn at the same scale. The filled dot is where the pen goes down.

What the robot receives

The output is a plain iRC program. Positions are stored once as named variables, then a list of linear moves refers to them.

The pen travels at Z = 100 mm and draws at Z = 20 mm, with the tool pointing straight down. Drawing moves run at half the travel speed.

Master's thesis · SRH Berlin · 2026

Can a robot navigate without a map?

I trained a mobile robot to reach its goal using only a LIDAR scan, then measured it against two classic planners that are handed the complete map.

Arena
50 × 50 m

Simulated arena. Start and goal sit 56.57 m apart.

Only sensor
24 beams

A 360° LIDAR is all the learned policy sees. It gets no map.

Training steps
500,000

Training steps, finished in 81 minutes on a laptop CPU.

Goal reached
4 of 8

Recorded runs reached the goal after training.

The question

A* and D* Lite find the shortest route every time, as long as someone gives them a complete map first. Warehouses and factory floors rarely stay the way they were mapped.

I wanted to know how close a robot gets when it has to learn the route from its own sensor readings, under the same robot model, arena, start and goal.

01

A simulation of the robot

An AgileX Scout Mini as a skid-steer model with motor lag, wall and obstacle collisions, and a 24-beam LIDAR with range noise.

02

Three ways to get there

A PPO policy trained with Stable-Baselines3, plus A* and D* Lite implemented from scratch on a shared occupancy grid.

03

A viewer to compare them

A browser-based 3D replay with live LIDAR, telemetry and all three paths, generated from the run data by a Python script.

Learning in three stages

The policy started with 12 obstacles in the arena, moved to 18 a third of the way through, and to 30 for the final third.

Mean episode reward climbed from −51 to +387 across 563 episodes. The dip at 330,000 steps lines up with the jump to 30 obstacles. The policy recovers by the end of the run.

Reward curve. Mean reward per episode with a 50-episode moving average. The dip near 330,000 steps is the switch to 30 obstacles.

Training setup. Robot, arena, sensor and PPO settings as logged at the start of the 500,000-step run.

With the full map, A* is hard to beat: the shortest path in under half a millisecond. D* Lite finds the same path and takes about six times longer for the first plan. It is built for maps that change mid-run, which a static arena never asks for.

The learned policy never saw the map. Its eight recorded runs averaged 61.6 m of driving against the 56.57 m shortest path, and four of them arrived.

The path lengths are not a like-for-like race: the planners ran on a 5-obstacle version of the arena, while the policy’s recorded runs faced all 30 obstacles.

No single method wins everywhere. The choice comes down to three questions: is a map available, do obstacles move, and is there time to train?

Where it falls short

The four runs that failed were still 9 to 12 m from the goal when the 900-step limit ended the episode. That limit allows 67.5 m of driving for a 56.57 m straight line.

What I would do next

  • Train longer, allow more stepsOne million training steps and a 1,200-step episode limit.
  • Try a more sample-efficient learnerSoft Actor-Critic in place of PPO.
  • Combine the two approachesA* for the global route, the learned policy for local manoeuvring.
  • Test with moving obstaclesThe case D* Lite's replanning is designed for.
  • Move to hardwareRun the policy on a real Scout Mini through ROS 2 and Gazebo.

Tech specs

Robot

  • AgileX Scout Mini, skid-steer
  • Top speed 1.5 m/s
  • Track width 0.49 m
  • Body radius 0.22 m

Arena

  • 50 × 50 m, walled
  • Start (−20, −20), goal (20, 20)
  • Goal radius 1.5 m
  • 0.05 s control step, 900 steps per episode

Sensing

  • 24-beam LIDAR, 360°
  • Range 15 m
  • Gaussian range noise, σ = 0.02 m
  • 35 inputs: 7 state, 24 LIDAR, 4 goal

Policy

  • PPO, Stable-Baselines3
  • MLP, 2 hidden layers of 256
  • 150,789 parameters
  • 2 outputs: left and right wheel speed

Training

  • 500,000 steps, 6 parallel environments
  • Curriculum: 12, 18, 30 obstacles
  • Discount 0.995, learning rate 3e-4
  • Entropy coefficient 0.05 to 0.003
  • Batch 256, 10 epochs, clip 0.2
  • 80.7 min, MacBook Pro, CPU only

Planners

  • A* with octile-distance heuristic
  • D* Lite (Koenig and Likhachev, 2002)
  • 100 × 100 grid, 0.5 m cells
  • 8-connected, obstacles inflated 0.25 m

Software

  • Python 3.13, NumPy
  • Stable-Baselines3 2.7, Gymnasium, PyTorch
  • three.js and Chart.js for the viewer
